1058.title: Looking back: the hard century
1058.hook: Banda, the forests, the ghallugharas, the misls
1058.howItsDone: The Ardas, said standing at the end of Sikh gatherings and prayers at home, includes a section remembering the martyrs and those who suffered for the faith; Sikhs also mark the ghallugharas and Banda Singh Bahadur's story on days in the calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the scribe, the storytellers and the saints, and your line was the tellers. Whose story did you hear to the end? Today, the stretch of the story that was hardest to tell. Day one thousand fifty-eight.

Cut limb from limb. Scalped. Broken on the wheel. Sawn apart. Those words sit inside the Ardas, the prayer Sikhs say standing, in a long remembering of people who, it says, kept their faith and their hair to the last breath. Every time the Ardas is said, in a home or a gurdwara, those people are remembered again. Tradition ties those lines to martyrs of the century after the Tenth Guru. This year, slowly, we heard their stories. Today, looking back at the hard century.
screen: `A REMEMBERING INSIDE THE ARDAS.` → `SAID AGAIN, EVERY TIME.` → `THE CENTURY AFTER THE TENTH GURU.`

segments.voice: It starts with a servant. At Nanded, a Bairagi ascetic named Madho Das met Guru Gobind Singh and, tradition says, called himself the Guru's banda, his servant. The Guru sent him north with five arrows. He took Sirhind, struck coins in the Gurus' names, and gave land to the farmers who worked it. Then came the hunt: the hills, a starving siege in a mud fort, capture, the march to Delhi, and a death that tradition says he met without breaking. Next, the forests. With rulers hunting them, Sikhs took to the jungles and the hills, on horseback, and tradition says they slipped out to visit the Harmandir at night when they could. Bhai Mani Singh, Bhai Taru Singh, and others whose deaths stand behind those Ardas lines belong to this time. Then the ghallugharas, the name Sikhs give to the great killings. At Kup Rahira, Sikhs remember how the Khalsa fought while keeping the women, children and elders in the middle of them, shielding the families as they moved. And through it all, the misls. Even before the worst of the killings, the Sikhs had organized into bands of equals, each with its own chief, joined together in the Dal Khalsa. They met at Amritsar, and decisions taken there in the Guru's presence were called gurmata. By the end of the century the hunted were holding the land. That's the arc: a servant, the forests, the great killings, and bands of equals. Today's line: the hard century.

segments.voice: Two minutes for the martyrs. Sit still, feet on the floor, and slow down. The practice is the part of the Ardas that remembers them. If you pray and know those lines, you can say them now, quietly, in Punjabi or in your own understanding of them. If you don't, simply hold the picture in silence: the people of that century, the families in the middle of the ring, the ones who kept going. Let each breath out be a small bow to them. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Today at the century after the Tenth Guru: Banda's rise and death, the years in the forests, the ghallugharas, and the misls. Today's word.

Your line: the hard century. If you hear the Ardas today, or say it, listen for the martyrs' lines. If not, give one minute of quiet to the people who carried the Sikh story through it. Day one thousand fifty-eight.

1059.title: Looking back: kingdom and loss
1059.hook: Ranjit Singh's Punjab, the wars and the exiles
1059.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharaja Ranjit Singh's rule and the fall of the Sikh kingdom in histories, songs and gatherings; the gilded Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar remains a living center of Sikh worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the hard century, from Banda to the misls, and your line was the hard century. Did you give the martyrs a minute? Today, what came after it: a kingdom, and its end. Day one thousand fifty-nine.

Gold, on a temple roof in Amritsar, catching the morning light. A great diamond, wrapped and carried away across the sea. A mother, sent away from her young son. A boy, growing up among strangers, far from Punjab. Those four pictures hold a whole chapter of this year. The son of a misl chief became a Maharaja, built a kingdom, and covered the Harmandir in gold. After his death, almost everything he built was lost. Almost. Today, looking back at kingdom and loss.
screen: `GOLD ON A TEMPLE ROOF.` → `A DIAMOND CARRIED AWAY.` → `A MOTHER AND SON APART.`

segments.voice: First, the kingdom. Ranjit Singh rose from the Sukerchakia misl, entered Lahore, and was crowned Maharaja. He called his government the Sarkar-e-Khalsa, the Khalsa's government, and struck coins in the Gurus' names, not his own. He trained a modern army and covered the Harmandir in gilded copper and marble. In English, it came to be called the Golden Temple. Second, the wars. After his death came quarrels at court and then wars with the British. At Sobraon the Sikh army was defeated, and Sikh memory holds that some of its own commanders betrayed it. At Chillianwala it held its ground. At Gujrat it lost, and Punjab was annexed. Third, the exiles. Maharani Jind Kaur was separated from her son and sent away. The Koh-i-Noor diamond was taken from the boy king, Duleep Singh, and sent to Queen Victoria. He was raised by British guardians, far from home, and baptized a Christian. Fourth, what was kept. The kingdom ended, but the Harmandir still shines. The Granth was still read, the Ardas still said, the langar still served. And the boy, grown up, went looking for the faith he'd been taken from. A kingdom can be signed away on paper. A faith, it turned out, was harder to take. Today's line: lost and kept.
screen: `THE KINGDOM: THE KHALSA'S GOVERNMENT.` · `THE WARS: DEFEAT AND ANNEXATION.` · `THE EXILES: A QUEEN, A DIAMOND, A BOY.` · `WHAT WAS KEPT.` · then, large: `LOST AND KEPT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with two lists. Sit back and let the breath settle. On one side, let something you've lost come to mind: a place, a person, a role, a time of life. Don't argue with it. Just let it be named. Then, on the other side, look for what you kept through that loss: a habit, a love, a word, a way of being. Hold both, one in each hand. If you pray, you can say Waheguru over each one. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Today at Ranjit Singh's Punjab, the wars with the British, the exiles of a queen, a diamond and a boy, and what survived the end of the kingdom. Today's word.
Your line: lost and kept. Today, when you notice something missing, a thing, a habit, a person's voice, look straight after for one thing that stayed. Day one thousand fifty-nine.

1060.title: Looking back: renewal and today
1060.hook: reform, peaceful protest, 1947, 1984, and the Sikhs of every continent
1060.howItsDone: The Ardas closes by asking for chardi kala, rising spirits, through the Name, and sarbat da bhala, the good of all; Sikhs in Punjab and far beyond say it at the end of prayers and gatherings, and remember Partition and 1984 in gatherings each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at kingdom and loss, and your line was lost and kept. What did you notice that stayed? Today, the last stretch of the long story, the one still being written. Day one thousand sixty.

Near the close of the Ardas, wherever it's said, come two words. Chardi kala. Rising spirits, high spirits, a spirit that keeps climbing. Sikhs say it in a gurdwara in Amritsar, in a living room in a cold country, beside a hospital bed, at a wedding. After the kingdom was gone, the Sikh story could have shrunk to a memory. It didn't. It renewed itself, suffered again, and spread far from Punjab. Today, looking back at renewal and today.
screen: `NEAR THE ARDAS'S CLOSE: CHARDI KALA.` → `SAID WHEREVER THE ARDAS IS SAID.` → `THE STORY DIDN'T SHRINK.`

segments.voice: First, renewal. Reformers rose: Baba Dayal calling Sikhs back to the formless God, the Namdharis in white, and the Singh Sabhas founding schools, presses and study circles to renew Sikh learning. Second, peaceful protest. When Sikhs set out to free their gurdwaras from the mahants, hereditary custodians the reformers accused of misrule, protesters pledged not to strike back, and took the blows. Nankana remembers peaceful martyrs. Later came a long campaign for a Punjabi-speaking state. Third, the wounds. Partition split Punjab. Villages burned, trains of refugees crossed the new border, violence struck on every side, and Guru Nanak's birthplace was left on the far side of the line. Families started again from nothing. And then what Sikhs simply call 1984: the army's assault on the Harmandir complex, and the killings of Sikhs in Delhi and other cities that followed. It is still a wound, still remembered with care. Fourth, today. Sikhs now live far from Punjab, in many countries, building gurdwaras, opening langars to whoever walks in, serving in disasters with food and water. And right after chardi kala, the Ardas ends with one more phrase: sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Not of Sikhs alone. Of everyone. That's where the long story stands now: renewed, wounded, and spread out, still asking for the good of all. Today's line: everywhere, still rising.
screen: `RENEWAL: REFORMERS AND SCHOOLS.` · `PEACEFUL PROTEST: BLOWS NOT RETURNED.` · `THE WOUNDS: PARTITION AND 1984.` · `TODAY: FAR FROM PUNJAB, SERVING ALL.` · then, large: `EVERYWHERE, STILL RISING.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for Sikhs everywhere. Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind the places from today: Amritsar, Nankana, a village rebuilt, a gurdwara in a city far away, a volunteer handing out food after a storm. If you pray, you can pray for Sikhs everywhere, for their safety and their chardi kala, and you can hold the Ardas's last wish with them, sarbat da bhala, the good of all. If you don't pray, simply wish them well, one place at a time, on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Today at the reformers, the peaceful protesters, the wounds of Partition and 1984, and the Sikhs who now live far from Punjab, still saying chardi kala. Today's word.
Your line: everywhere, still rising. Today, if you pass a gurdwara or meet a Sikh neighbor, a classmate or a coworker, let the whole long story stand behind them for a moment. Day one thousand sixty.

1061.title: Year three close
1061.hook: the long story is told; next year, the ways of the Guru: ragas, teachings, and the living panth
1061.howItsDone: In the Ardas, said standing at the end of Sikh prayers and gatherings, Sikhs remember the Gurus, the Sahibzade, the Panj Pyare, the forty liberated ones and the martyrs before making their requests, so the community's history is recalled every time it is said.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at renewal and today, and your line was everywhere, still rising. Who did you wish well? Today is the last day of year three. Day one thousand sixty-one.

A storyteller's Nanak. A weaver's songs in the Guru's book. A servant sent north. Families shielded in a moving ring. A gold roof, a boy far from home, protesters who didn't strike back, a kitchen that feeds whoever comes. That's this year, said in one breath, from day six hundred ninety-seven, when Bhai Gurdas opened it, to this one. Each picture is a name that became a story. Today: year three close.
screen: `A STORYTELLER, A WEAVER, A SERVANT.` → `A YEAR IN ONE BREATH.` → `NAMES THAT BECAME STORIES.`

segments.voice: Look at the shape of it. Year one gave you the path's words, stories, practices and the Japji. Year two gave you the daily banis, a day lived in the Guru's words. Year three gave you a people's memory. It began with the tellers: Bhai Gurdas, Bhai Nand Lal, the janamsakhis, and the Bhagats. Then the people around the Gurus. Then the hard century, the misls, the kingdom and its loss. Then reform, the twentieth century, and the calendar of days on which Sikhs remember. Why spend a whole year on history? Listen to the Ardas. Before it asks for anything, it remembers: the Gurus by name, the four Sahibzade, the five beloved ones, the forty liberated ones, and the martyrs who kept their faith. Every time a Sikh stands for the Ardas, the long story is told again in a few minutes. So the history isn't a school subject sitting beside the faith. It's inside the prayer. Whoever stands for the Ardas stands among everyone it names. That's today's line: the story holds us. Now turn and face the other way. Year four is the ways of the Guru: the ragas the Granth is set in, the teachings opened slowly, and the living panth, the community as it lives now. Tomorrow begins with a question about sound, and why the Gurus' words were meant to be sung. The faces from this year won't vanish. Bhai Gurdas's vars, for one, are sung in kirtan beside the Guru's words.
screen: `THREE YEARS: WORDS, A DAY, A MEMORY.` · `THE ARDAS TELLS THE STORY AGAIN.` · `HISTORY INSIDE THE PRAYER.` · `YEAR FOUR: THE WAYS OF THE GURU.` · then, large: `THE STORY HOLDS US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest, and look ahead. Lean back. Let the shoulders drop and the jaw loosen. For a while, do nothing at all. Let the year settle: the tellers, the martyrs, the kings, the exiles, the kitchens. No need to sort it. Then, toward the end, look forward to tomorrow, and to a sound: a harmonium, a voice, a line of the Guru's words set to music. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, as thanks for the year. If you don't, simply let tomorrow have some room in it. The bell holds the time.
Year three close. The end of the long story: the tellers, the saints, the hard century, the kingdom and its loss, renewal and today, with the ways of the Guru ahead. Today's word.
Your line: the story holds us. Tonight, tell one story from this year to someone, at the table or on the phone, and let it be told well and truly. Day one thousand sixty-one. Year three, done.
